opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core of it comes from a fairly simple observation: talent is evenly distributed around the world, but opportunity really isn't. When you look at where machine learning research happens, it's concentrated in a handful of places, a few cities and a few institutions, and that shapes which questions get asked and who gets to ask them.

My own path was pretty nontraditional. I grew up across Africa, and I started a nonprofit focused on machine learning before I went to Google Brain. So I've felt firsthand how hard it is to break into this field if you're not in the right zip code or don't have the right pedigree. When we set up Cohere For AI, we wanted the lab to be a deliberate experiment in changing where research comes from.

So we have two halves. One is a more traditional research lab that works on fundamental questions: efficiency, robustness, how models behave at scale, multilingual work. The other is an open science community, which is now thousands of researchers across well over a hundred countries. People join from everywhere: independent researchers, students, people working in industry who want to do research on the side. We run reading groups, mentorship, and research collaborations, and a lot of that work ends up as published papers.

I think there's a real scientific payoff to that, not only a fairness one. Our Aya project is a good example. We wanted to build a massively multilingual model, and you simply can't do that well from one lab in one country. You need native speakers, people who understand the cultural context and know where the data gaps are. It ended up being thousands of collaborators contributing across a huge number of languages. That kind of work only happens if you build the infrastructure for open, distributed collaboration from the start.

More broadly, I think the field benefits when more people are at the table. Many of the blind spots in our models, which languages they underserve, whose norms they encode, come from the narrowness of who builds them. Widening that circle is one of the most practical things we can do to make the technology better and more representative.

r001.rationale: The response describes globally distributed talent and an international research community, but does not clearly identify worldwide recruitment as a way to access exceptional ML talent through a larger pool.

r002.rationale: Google Brain appears only in the speaker’s biography; the response does not argue that Cohere for AI should pursue distinctive research instead of reproducing its work.

r003.rationale: It presents open, distributed collaboration as enabling work that a single lab could not do, using the multilingual Aya project as an example.

r004.rationale: It says Cohere for AI aimed to change where research comes from and that multilingual work requires collaborators and infrastructure beyond one lab in one country.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest starting point is that I don't believe the next big ideas in machine learning are going to come from a handful of zip codes. If you look at where talent actually sits in the world, it's incredibly distributed, but where the resources sit, where the compute is, where the mentorship is, where the paper-writing know-how is, that's incredibly concentrated. So there's this huge gap between who could contribute and who actually gets the chance to.

When we set up Cohere for AI, the question I kept asking was, what does a research lab look like if you design it from the ground up around that gap rather than ignoring it? And the answer we arrived at is a kind of hybrid. We have a core research team that works on fundamental questions, things like efficiency, data, how models generalize. But alongside that we have an open science community, which is now thousands of people across well over a hundred countries. A lot of them have never published before. Some are coming from fields outside of ML entirely. What we provide is structure, compute, and mentorship, and what they bring is perspectives we would never have inside a single office.

The "open collaboration" piece matters to me for a slightly different reason, which is that I think a lot of progress in our field is being bottlenecked by who gets to participate rather than by ideas. Multilingual work is a great example. If you want a model that actually works well in Swahili or Telugu or Vietnamese, the people who can tell you whether it's good are not sitting in San Francisco. Projects like Aya came directly out of that realization. Three thousand people contributing data and evaluation for over a hundred languages is not something you can do with a closed team, no matter how talented.

I'll also say there's a selfish research argument here. Many of the problems I care about, like why models fail on rare examples, or how to do more with less compute, are exactly the problems that look very different depending on where you're standing. Someone training models on a single GPU in Lagos has a very different intuition about efficiency than someone with a cluster. I think that diversity of constraints produces better science, not just more inclusive science.

And the last thing is that it's an experiment. I don't think we have the perfect recipe. Coordinating distributed research is hard, time zones are hard, keeping quality high while opening the door wide is hard. But I'd rather be running that experiment and learning from it than defaulting to the structure every other lab has, because I think that default is leaving an enormous amount of talent on the table.

r001.rationale: The response says talent is distributed worldwide and describes a community spanning over a hundred countries, giving people who lack access to research resources a chance to contribute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Google Brain or argue against reproducing its research.

r003.rationale: It presents open science collaboration as enabling work a closed team could not do, including multilingual research, and says varied perspectives and constraints produce better science.

r004.rationale: It argues for designing a hybrid lab around distributed participation, providing structure, compute, and mentorship, and says research benefits from varied settings and constraints.

astra-6.text:
The starting point for me is that talent is everywhere, but access to the opportunity to do research is not. If we recruit only from a handful of universities or places, we’re missing people who could make really important contributions. And we’re also narrowing the questions we ask, because people’s experiences shape which problems they notice and want to solve.

With Cohere for AI, I wanted us to think deliberately about how to lower those barriers. Can someone participate in a research community without moving countries or already knowing the right people? Can they find collaborators, develop an idea, and get feedback that helps them do rigorous work?

Open collaboration is a big part of that. Making research accessible matters, but so does creating a way for people to contribute. That takes effort when people are distributed across time zones and have different resources available to them. You have to build for that participation.

For me, the ambition is both to broaden who gets to do research and to make the research better. A community with a wider range of perspectives can challenge assumptions that a more concentrated group might never think to question.

r001.rationale: The response says talent is everywhere and recruiting narrowly misses people who could contribute, but it does not clearly identify exceptional ML talent or a larger talent pool as the reason for worldwide recruitment.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Google Brain or argue that Cohere for AI should pursue distinctive research instead of reproducing it.

r003.rationale: It presents open collaboration and broader participation as ways to bring in perspectives that challenge assumptions and improve the research, conveying a different kind of research.

r004.rationale: It argues for lowering participation barriers and building research practices that work across time zones and resource differences, which communicates changing the settings in which research is done.

sol-6.1.text:
The thinking is that talent is everywhere, but access to the resources needed to contribute to AI research is not. If you build a research community around a handful of institutions or geographic hubs, you miss people with very different experiences, questions, and ideas.

For me, open collaboration is about making it possible for those people to do meaningful research together. That takes more than putting something online. You need a community where people can ask questions, find collaborators, and develop the confidence to contribute, even if they haven’t followed a traditional path into research.

And that matters for the research itself. When you have people coming from different contexts, they challenge your assumptions about what problems are important and who these systems should work for. We want that breadth of perspective to be part of how the work gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says talent is everywhere and access to research resources is uneven, but it does not identify worldwide recruitment as a way to reach exceptional ML talent through a larger pool.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss pursuing distinctive research or contrast Cohere for AI with Google Brain.

r003.rationale: It says open collaboration brings people from different contexts together, challenging assumptions about important problems and who systems should serve, presenting collaboration as shaping the research.

r004.rationale: The response calls for a supportive community that enables meaningful research, but does not argue that Cohere for AI must change the settings in which research is done.
